<reason>Both sides argued sharply and both suffered clipped turns, but PRO (B) built the cleaner decision rule and defended it under pressure. B's core weighing—escalation by the responder is a recurring, documented mechanism of death, while the "sister harmed in the gap" is a hypothetical CON had to construct—survived to the end, and B neutralized CON's strongest specific (the overdose) by showing expansion adds alongside EMS rather than replacing it. B also answered both pressure questions directly (dispatch tiers as the bound; overdose untouched) and then turned CON's own concession that officers are "trainable" into the decisive line: an undated promissory note versus a program cities can run now. CON's best surviving material was the imperfect-triage point ("dispatch hears pacing, not the knife") and the "bounce" mechanism, which is real, but CON never quantified or grounded how often mislabeled wellness checks turn lethal in the added minutes, and its answer to B's training-timeline question ("wait on neither") dodged the date. CON's rhetoric was excellent, but B's frame made the motion easier to decide as written: the "even if" is bounded to non-lethal tiers, whereas CON's alternative is unbounded.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's Rebuttal 2 answering A's overdose question—showing the clinician team is added alongside EMS so the overdose is untouched, that the officer's gap tasks (rescue breaths, blocking a lane) require no gun and are already coached over the phone, and that the only death speed uniquely prevents is hypothetical while the raised-blade shooting recurs with the officer already fast. CON's "swap" counter was coherent but B's closing (wellness check rerouted, overdose not) held the line.</best_rebuttal>
